title: Judges 20:1–17
context: Israel assembles as one man at Mizpah, from Dan to Beersheba, to hear what happened. The Levite gives his account, which differs from the narrative of chapter 19 at several points, most notably in leaving out that he himself forced his concubine outside. The tribes resolve to punish Gibeah and ask Benjamin to hand over the guilty men, but Benjamin refuses and gathers to defend Gibeah, setting the stage for civil war. The very large army numbers in this chapter are understood in more than one way by interpreters. Readers in both traditions commonly see here a just cause handled amid deep confusion, a community rightly outraged at evil yet heading toward catastrophic violence.

verses.text: Then all the children of Israel went out, and the congregation was assembled as one man, from Dan even to Beersheba, with the land of Gilead, to the LORD at Mizpah.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the whole people gathering as one man at Mizpah, from Dan to Beersheba. The outrage at Gibeah unites the tribes as rarely happens in Judges.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the striking unity of the assembly before the LORD. Both traditions commonly see this unity as a right response to evil that will nonetheless lead into tragic excess.

verses.text: The chiefs of all the people, even of all the tribes of Israel, presented themselves in the assembly of the people of God, four hundred thousand footmen who drew sword.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the large number of armed men presented in the assembly. Interpreters understand these large figures in more than one way, and readers need not press them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the assembly of the people of God as a formal gathering to address a grave crime. Readers in both traditions commonly hold the numbers with caution while affirming the seriousness of the moment.

verses.text: (Now the children of Benjamin heard that the children of Israel had gone up to Mizpah.) The children of Israel said, “Tell us, how did this wickedness happen?”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Benjamin hears of the gathering but is apparently not present. The assembly asks how this wickedness happened, seeking the truth.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the inquiry as a proper first step toward justice (compare Deuteronomy 13:14). Both traditions commonly read the verse as setting up the Levite’s testimony.

verses.text: The Levite, the husband of the woman who was murdered, answered, “I came into Gibeah that belongs to Benjamin, I and my concubine, to spend the night.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that the narrator calls the Levite the husband of the woman who was murdered, naming her death plainly. His testimony begins with his arrival in Gibeah.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the narrator’s description as a moral clarification even before the Levite speaks. Readers in both traditions commonly read his account alongside chapter 19 to see what he includes and what he leaves out.

verses.text: The men of Gibeah rose against me, and surrounded the house by night. They intended to kill me and they raped my concubine, and she is dead.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice that the Levite says the men intended to kill him and that they raped his concubine, but he does not mention that he forced her out. His account protects his own reputation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise observe the selective nature of his testimony compared with the narrative. Both traditions commonly read the gap as part of the narrator’s critique of the Levite, while acknowledging that the crime of the men of Gibeah was real.

verses.text: I took my concubine and cut her in pieces, and sent her throughout all the country of the inheritance of Israel; for they have committed lewdness and folly in Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite describing his act of cutting her in pieces as a summons to address lewdness and folly in Israel. He frames himself as the wronged party.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that he names the crime correctly as lewdness and folly yet remains silent on his own role. Readers in both traditions commonly see the verse as a reminder that people can rightly condemn evil while concealing their own share in it.

verses.text: Behold, you children of Israel, all of you, give here your advice and counsel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the Levite calling all Israel to give advice and counsel. The decision about how to respond to this evil now rests with the whole assembly.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the appeal as placing responsibility on the whole community. Both traditions commonly read the verse as the point where the assembly must choose how to respond.

verses.text: All the people arose as one man, saying, “None of us will go to his tent, neither will any of us turn to his house.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the people rising as one man and vowing not to return home until the matter is addressed. Their resolve is strong and immediate.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the united resolve as a fitting response to grave evil, though one that will later be shaped by rash oaths. Readers in both traditions commonly see the danger of acting in collective anger without restraint.

verses.text: But now this is the thing which we will do to Gibeah: we will go up against it by lot;
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the plan to go up against Gibeah by lot, a practice used to seek order and fairness. The people intend to act deliberately.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the use of the lot as a recognized way of decision-making in Israel. Both traditions commonly read the verse as part of a plan that is orderly in form but will become devastating in result.

verses.text: and we will take ten men of one hundred throughout all the tribes of Israel, and one hundred of one thousand, and a thousand out of ten thousand to get food for the people, that they may do, when they come to Gibeah of Benjamin, according to all the folly that the men of Gibeah have done in Israel.”
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note the provision of supplies for the army so that justice can be carried out against Gibeah for its folly. The community organizes itself carefully.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the plan as aimed at punishing Gibeah specifically for its crime. Readers in both traditions commonly observe that the stated goal is narrower than the destruction that eventually follows.

verses.text: So all the men of Israel were gathered against the city, knit together as one man.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the men of Israel knit together as one man against the city. Their unity is impressive, yet unity alone does not guarantee wisdom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the remarkable unity, which contrasts with the divisions elsewhere in Judges. Both traditions commonly read the verse as a high point of collective resolve before the tragedy unfolds.

verses.text: The tribes of Israel sent men through all the tribe of Benjamin, saying, “What wickedness is this that has happened among you?
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see the tribes sending messengers to Benjamin to ask about the wickedness among them. They first seek a peaceful resolution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see this approach as a right step, giving Benjamin the opportunity to address the crime (compare Matthew 18:15). Readers in both traditions commonly value the attempt to resolve the matter before war.

verses.text: Now therefore deliver up the men, the wicked fellows who are in Gibeah, that we may put them to death and put away evil from Israel.” But Benjamin would not listen to the voice of their brothers, the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers see Israel asking Benjamin to hand over the guilty men so evil can be put away. Benjamin’s refusal turns a crime by some into a conflict with a whole tribe.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see Benjamin’s refusal as siding with the guilty rather than with justice (compare Proverbs 17:15). Both traditions commonly read this as the decisive failure that leads to war.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin gathered themselves together out of the cities to Gibeah, to go out to battle against the children of Israel.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note that Benjamin gathers to Gibeah to fight their fellow Israelites. Loyalty to their own overrides concern for justice.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see tribal loyalty here hardening into resistance against what is right. Readers in both traditions commonly see a warning against defending wrongdoers simply because they belong to one’s own group.

verses.text: The children of Benjamin were counted on that day out of the cities twenty-six thousand men who drew the sword, in addition to the inhabitants of Gibeah, who were counted seven hundred chosen men.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Benjamin’s count of twenty-six thousand men plus seven hundred from Gibeah. These figures do not fully match later totals in the chapter, and interpreters explain the difference in various ways.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hold the numbers with caution while noting the narrator’s interest in Benjamin’s strength. Both traditions commonly read the verse as showing that Benjamin was a formidable opponent despite its smaller size.

verses.text: Among all these soldiers there were seven hundred chosen men who were left-handed. Every one of them could sling a stone at a hair and not miss.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers notice the seven hundred left-handed slingers who could sling a stone at a hair and not miss. Benjamin was known for skilled fighters (compare Judges 3:15; 1 Chronicles 12:2).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the detail as explaining Benjamin’s early success in battle. Readers in both traditions commonly read it as part of the narrative’s realism rather than as a point of doctrine.

verses.text: The men of Israel, besides Benjamin, were counted four hundred thousand men who drew sword. All these were men of war.
verses.arminianNotes: Arminian readers note Israel’s much larger force of four hundred thousand men of war. The disparity makes the early defeats in the next section all the more striking.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the large numbers as setting up the narrative tension of the battles that follow. Both traditions commonly read the figures with caution and focus on the story’s moral and spiritual shape.
